# spec

Design requirements for the delulu-smash app (`services/ui`), kept apart from `services/ui/README.md`,
which documents what is built. One file per concern. The spec says what must hold, the README says what
does.

## The spirit of the app

> *The simplicity & efficiency of Omarchy, the exploration of Jupyter, the composability of VS Code, and the
> extensibility & flexibility of Pi: your desktop hub.*

This is the app's mantra (the user's, Nov 2026), and every rule in this spec serves it. Each new feature and
design choice gets checked against all five parts. When one is traded off for another, say so.

| Part | What it means here | Already in the app |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Simplicity & efficiency of Omarchy** | Keyboard first, one letter per action, nothing on screen that isn't needed, every list searchable. It looks and behaves like the desktop around it | `Alt` keys, `Alt+K` list, `Alt+P` palette, panels hidden until wanted ([omarchy.md](omarchy.md)) |
| **Exploration of Jupyter** | Every result is a live value you can keep, poke at and build on, in the AI chat or in code. Asking a question and working on the answer are one flow | results as `r1`, `r2`, … ; Python cells; Variables panel; `@name` mentions ([variables.md](variables.md)) |
| **Composability of VS Code** | Pieces combine and rearrange instead of each living in one fixed place: panels are shown, hidden, split and zoomed to fit the task; a widget is the same wherever it is put (a Results tab, the chat, under a cell, floating); one value flows between the chat, the cells and the widgets; every action, whatever adds it, sits in the same palette and keys | panels with `Alt` keys and ⤢ / ×; widgets in tabs, chat, cells, Alt+F floating; `r1` used in cells and `@r1` in the chat; the `Alt+P` palette and slash commands |
| **Extensibility & flexibility of Pi** | As with the Pi coding agent: a small core that grows by adding pieces (widgets, tools, commands) as data, not by editing the core. The user shapes it to their own workflow, and the AI helps build the new pieces | `WIDGETS` rows, the palette / slash commands made from them, inline AI filling any widget's inputs ([inline_ai.md](inline_ai.md)) |
| **Your desktop hub** | One place for Smash work (data, VODs, AI, code), always running as a desktop app and not a site you visit | `SUPER+SHIFT+J`, `delulu-smash.service` |

## Words: panel and widget

Two different things, and the design rules differ for each. Use these words (the user's, Nov 2026); older text
and the code say "pane" for a panel.

| | Panel | Widget |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | a fixed region of the window's layout: a place | a view of one value: a thing shown in a place |
| Which | Chat, Results, Python, Variables, Terminal (experiment) | table, VODs, player usage, fields, SmashDb console, Browser |
| How many | one of each; shown or hidden (the bottom bar, `Alt` keys) | any number; the same value can be shown in several places |
| Where defined | the layout in `ui/ui.py` | a row in `WIDGETS` (`ui/widgets.py`), drawn by `render.py` |
| Holds | widgets, cells, messages | its own controls and state (filter, sort, inputs) |

Design rules that follow from the difference:

- **Panels are flush and uniform.** They touch their neighbours with one dividing line, no gap and no frame of
  their own, and the strip at the top of each is the same height (`--panel-head` in `assets/app.css`), so they
  line up when several are open.
- **A widget is self-contained and the same wherever it is placed** (a Results tab, the chat, under a cell):
  it keeps its own frame and brings its controls with it. See the README's "Rendering" design rule.
- **Widgets are flush and square too**, as the Omarchy desktop (gaps 0, rounding 0; Nov 2026): no space
  around a widget in any place, and square corners (`--widget-gap` / `--widget-radius` in `assets/app.css`,
  the one setting for every place). Its frame is a 1px line, **except where it fills a place** (a Results
  tab): there the place's lines frame it, so there is one line, as between panels. Under a cell it keeps its
  indent, lined up with the code.
- A new region of the window is a panel; a new way to show a value is a widget. Don't give a panel a widget's
  frame, or build a widget that only works in one panel.
- **Toggles don't move the content.** Opening or closing something (a box, a row, a status) never shifts what
  is already on screen. So the inline AI box (`Alt+I`, or the strip's ✨) opens in the title strip of the panel
  or widget it acts on, in the strip's free width left of its buttons; Esc, `Alt+I` again or the lit ✨ close
  it and put the cursor back. **Exception: a console**: a Python cell's box opens under the cell it edits (the
  cell is its place). Today: a widget's inputs (`render.strip_ask_box`, in its bar), the Terminal
  (`ui.strip_ask` + `assets/frame_ask.js`: a framed page has no place of its own, so the app draws the box and
  the page only does its part, eg reading the screen and pasting the command); one look for all
  (`.inline-box` in `assets/app.css`).

## Widgets: three regions, the same for every widget

The user's rule (Nov 2026): every widget is built from the same three regions, top to bottom, **with no
exceptions** (not the Browser, not a playing video). As with panels, learning one widget teaches all of them.

> **Consistency beats a widget's own optimizations.** A few simple, fixed design and visual expectations make
> the app easy to find your way around, and matter more as widgets become dynamic and differ more. When a
> widget would be a little better with its own layout, it still follows the shared one.

```
│ MatchVideos  [✨ Ask AI box, when open]                       ✨  Inputs ▾  ⤢  × │  1. the bar
│ player 1 [DeLulu]  player 2 [   ]  char 1 [any ▾] …                         Run   │  2. the Inputs panel
│ [video] [video]                                                                   │  3. the display
│ … the widget's own design: results, its pager, its filters, a playing video …     │
```

| Region | Holds | Never |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. The bar** (the widget's top border) | only, in this order: its **name** (the tool's or the value's type, eg `MatchVideos`, `DataFrame`, `SmashDb`, `Browser`); the **inline AI** where the widget has it (✨, and its box in the bar's free width while open: "Toggles don't move the content" above); **Inputs ▸/▾** where it takes parameters; **⤢** (float / put back); **×** (close). The same height and look on every widget, always shown | anything else: no counts or status ("2 found", "120 rows", "not run yet"), no paging, filters, toggles or links of the widget's own |
| **2. The Inputs panel** | the widget's **parameters**, if it takes any: what it is run or loaded with, and Run. Folds under the bar (Inputs ▸/▾). A widget without parameters has no Inputs button and no panel | view controls (a table's row filter, sort, SQL): those aren't inputs ([inline_ai.md](inline_ai.md), "View controls are not inputs"), they belong to the display |
| **3. The display** | the widget's output, **designed and rendered by the widget itself**: its results and everything about them (counts and status, paging, a table's filter and SQL, a SmashDb console's History and Assign, the video player when a video is picked). Whatever it shows or opens stays inside this region | reaching outside its region: a picked video plays inside the display, it never replaces or hides the bar or the Inputs panel |

- **The display's own line is at its bottom.** A widget's status and its own controls (eg `2 found · page 1 of 1`
  with ‹ Prev / Next ›, a table's filter, SQL ▸ and `120 rows`), when it has them, sit in one line at the
  bottom of the display, like a status bar; the results start right under the bar (or the Inputs panel).
  The links of the place showing it (`↗ tab` in the chat and under a cell, `↖ chat` in a Results tab) end
  that line, after the widget's own controls.
- **Enforced in code, not by convention.** A widget supplies only its parts (its name, whether it has inline AI,
  its parameters, its display); the one shared frame (`render.py`) draws the bar and the Inputs panel from
  them, so a widget can't put anything else in its bar or skip a region.
- **A new widget** is a new display (and parameters, if it takes any) plugged into that frame, never a new bar.
- In the code: `render.widget_frame` is that frame (`widget_bar`, the Inputs panel, `widget_line`); a widget is
  a `WidgetParts` (display, its bottom line's controls, its own Inputs or ✨ when it has no tool form) under its
  kind in `render.PARTS`. `tests/services/ui/test_widget_frame.py` fails when a bar, an Inputs panel or a
  bottom line is drawn anywhere else, or a kind has no parts.

## Words: one word per action

The same action has the same word everywhere it appears: a button, a slash command, a palette entry, a form's
label and the docs. Learn the word once and it works in every place (the user's rule, Nov 2026).

- **A slash command's name is the word.** When an action already has one, the buttons and labels for that
  action use it. Eg binding a result to a Python name is `/assign`, so the SmashDb console's button is
  `Assign ▸` (it was "Save as"), its row reads "Assign result to" and its submit button "Assign".
- **Before naming a new control**, look for the action under another name (`ui/commands.py`, the slash
  commands, the other widgets' bars) and reuse that word. If nothing fits, the new word becomes the one to
  reuse.
- **Short**: one word where it can be ("Assign", not "Assign variable").
- Two controls that do different things don't share a word, even when they look alike.

## Icons: Nerd Font glyphs

Every icon in the app is a Nerd Font glyph: a character of the app's own mono font (JetBrainsMono Nerd
Font). **Don't use an SVG for an icon** (nor a PNG, nor an icon from another library such as Lucide), even
when it would be easier to centre (the user's rule, Nov 2026, after the AI icon was tried as an SVG and
taken out again).

**The font ships with the app** (`services/ui/assets/nerd_fonts/`, updated with `ds ui fonts`), so a
fresh clone draws every icon with no font installed, and a new icon needs no extra step: the whole font
is there. Why and how: `spec/services/ui/dependencies.md`.

Why:

- **One look.** The glyphs come from one family (mostly its Material Design set, `nf-md-*`), so they share
  a weight and a style. An icon from another library stands out beside them, in size and in line weight.
- **They line up.** A glyph is sized by the font size, like the text beside it.
- **They are text, so text effects work on them.** An icon takes the colour of what it is in (green for a
  panel that is open, grey for one that isn't), and an animation on the text applies to it too: the inline
  chat's icon pulses while the AI is working, after Enter, with no code for the icon itself.

Rules:

- **A new icon is a Nerd Font glyph**, from the Material set (`nf-md-*`) when it has one, so it matches the
  others. Look it up on the Nerd Fonts cheat sheet and name it in a comment next to its code point.
- **Defined once, by name**, in `ui/commands.py` (`ICON_TABLE`, `ICON_TERMINAL`, ...): the palette, the
  bottom bar and the buttons all draw the same constant.
- **One icon per meaning.** "The AI" is one icon everywhere it appears (`render.ai_icon`: the Chat toggle,
  the inline AI buttons, the "Ask AI" row, the inline chat box).
- **Centre it by its drawing, not its text cell.** A glyph is drawn from the left of its cell and is wider
  than it, so centred as text it hangs to the right. Put it in a box as wide as its drawing (as `.ai-icon`
  in `assets/app.css` does, with the measured width), so whatever centres the box centres the icon at any
  size. Don't nudge it per button: that is what kept breaking.
- **If no glyph fits, ask** before using anything else.

Not icons, so not covered: pictures of things (the app's mark, character portraits, video thumbnails).

## Panels: what every panel has

The same controls on every panel, so learning one teaches all of them (Omarchy's "one pattern everywhere").
A new panel gets all of these; a panel missing one is a bug.

| | Rule | Today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Key** | `Alt+<letter>` shows or hides it, from anywhere, **including from inside it**: a panel whose content takes the keyboard (the Terminal's shell) hands its own keys back to the app. Showing it by its key puts the cursor in it | `Alt+A` chat (AI), `Alt+R` Results, `Alt+J` Python (Jupyter), `Alt+V` Variables, ``Alt+` `` Terminal (VS Code's terminal key, Ctrl+\`, with the app's Alt), also `Alt+Enter` (Omarchy's `SUPER+Enter` opens a terminal) |
| **Full screen** | `Alt+Shift+<the same letter>` fills the window with it, from anywhere, even when hidden; the same key again puts the layout back. `Alt+F` does it for the panel you are in | `Alt+Shift+A` / `R` / `J` / `V` / `` ` `` (Terminal also `Alt+Shift+Enter`) |
| **Title strip** | the same height on every panel (`--panel-head`), flush with its neighbours; it ends with ⤢ (full screen) and × (close: the same as its key). Its title may be left out to keep the panel bare (the chat has none; its model is in the window's title bar) | `zoom_button`, `close_button` in `ui/ui.py` |
| **Bottom bar** | one toggle per panel, lit while it is shown, in panel order | 🤖 ▦ 🐍 ⚙ >_ |
| **Palette** | a "Show / Hide <panel>" row and a "Full screen: <panel>" row in `Alt+P` | `commands.py` |
| **Closing keeps it** | hiding a panel (key, ×, bottom bar) only hides it: what is in it stays (cells, variables, the shell). Only a page reload starts it over | `.is-hidden` (CSS), not unmounted |
| **Takes the space** | a panel whose neighbour is hidden takes the freed space; nothing leaves a gap | `*_layout` in `state.py` (hidden / alone / split) |
| **Defined once** | its keys in `ui/shortcuts.py` (so they show in `Alt+K` and the help), its name in `state.PANES` | |

Choosing a letter: Omarchy's own letter for the same action first (see [omarchy.md](omarchy.md)), else the
first letter that says what it is and is free (`J` for Jupyter because `P` is the palette), or the key
another tool the user knows uses for it (``Alt+` `` for the Terminal, from VS Code's Ctrl+\`).

## The app explains itself

The chat can answer how to use the app (`services/ui/guide.md`, loaded by the chat agent on demand). So:

- **A user-visible feature gets its lines in `guide.md`** in the same change: what to type and what shows,
  no file or function names. Short: the guide is sent whole to the model.
- Lists that exist as data (slash commands, keys) are added from the code, never retyped in the guide.
- The agent answers app questions from the guide only, and says when the guide doesn't cover something.

## Platforms: Omarchy (Arch Linux) and Windows

The user's rule (Nov 2026): the app is cross platform. It must run on **Omarchy (Arch Linux)**, where it is
built and has its window and service, and on **Windows**, where `ds ui install` gives it the same: a
Task Scheduler task at logon (per user, no admin), a desktop / Start Menu icon and Ctrl+Alt+J that open an
Edge app window (the user's choice, Nov 2026; before it was started by hand with `uv run reflex run`,
which still works). macOS is not a target: don't break it knowingly, but when it conflicts with the other two,
they win.

- **What "runs" means on Windows today**: `uv sync`, then `uv run reflex run`, and the page works: chat,
  Results, SmashDb, VODs, the Python cells, Variables, Config, the debug panel. With no keys stored it runs
  without the AI ("The app works without the AI" above).
- **Linux-only parts are extras, never requirements.** What comes from Omarchy (the wallpaper, the ghostty
  theme, `hyprctl`, the systemd service, `ds ui restart`, `.os/`) is used when it is there and skipped in
  silence when it isn't: a default, not an error.
- **A feature that can't work on a platform says so in its own place** and nothing else changes: no second
  layout, no hidden controls. Today: the **Terminal** panel on Windows (it needs a Unix pseudo-terminal):
  its page is one line saying so (`terminal.AVAILABLE`).
- **Rules for the code** (`pkgs/ds`, `services/ui/ui`; `tests/test_cross_platform.py` checks the first three):
  - Text files are read and written with `encoding="utf-8"` by name: Windows' default isn't UTF-8.
  - A Unix-only stdlib module (`fcntl`, `pty`, `termios`, `resource`, `pwd`, ...) is imported only inside
    `try: ... except ImportError`, with its absence handled; the whole app must import without them.
  - A package only Windows needs is a dependency with `sys_platform == 'win32'` (today `tzdata`).
  - Paths are built with `pathlib` from `Path.home()` or the repo, never a fixed `/usr/...` that must exist;
    an outside program is looked up and its absence handled.
- **Known gaps on Windows** (each fails in its own place; none stops the app):

  | What | On Windows |
  | --- | --- |
  | Terminal panel | not available: needs a pseudo-terminal backend for Windows (eg ConPTY) |
  | `from_url`'s browser fallback | looks for Chromium at `/usr/bin/chromium` only |
  | Spend view's days | start at UTC midnight (the local zone is read from `/etc/localtime`) |
  | Debug panel, System tab | no memory or open-file numbers (read from `/proc`) |
  | `os sync` | Omarchy's: not there (run `ds ui install` once per Windows machine instead) |
  | The window's hotkey | Ctrl+Alt+J (a shortcut's own hotkey: Windows allows Ctrl+Alt only), not SUPER+SHIFT+J |

- **How it is checked**: on Linux, by tests that stand in for Windows (the app imported with the Unix-only
  modules blocked for this repo's code) and a dry run that every locked package has a Windows build. That is
  not a run on Windows: say so, and say what was really run there, when reporting such work.

## Settings

The app's settings are one `Config` class (`services/ui/ui/config.py`) read from `services/ui/config.toml`.

- **A setting is a private variable plus a property that holds its default.** Adding one is those lines:
  its inputs, form, file key, `set_<name>` and Config tab row are derived, never written per setting.
- **Changed through `set_config`**, a function like any widget's tool: the Config widget's form and inline AI
  come from it. The user runs a change; the chat agent has no tool for it.
- **Hot reload, no cache**: a setting is read from the file on each use; a change shows without a restart.
- **A bad value changes nothing**, and a file that can't be used leaves the defaults and says why.
- **An on/off setting** (`-> bool`) is a checkbox in the form; while it equals its default it is "not set"
  (its key stays out of the file).

## The app works without the AI

The user's rule (Nov 2026): the app works without the AI. Everything that isn't the AI (SmashDb, tables,
VODs, the Python cells, the Terminal, the slash commands) must run without it, and with no key at all.

- **Kept simple** (the user's rule): no second mode of the app and no wording of its own for "the AI is
  off". What is the AI's is just not on the page, and a shared string is written once with its AI words
  left out (eg the chat box's hint). Don't add a branch, a label or a message per feature for this.
- **One question, one guard** (`services/ui/ui/ai_switch.py`): `ai_problem()` is "" when the AI may be
  used, else why not (the `allow_ai` setting isn't ticked, or what the model needs isn't stored: the same
  thing to the app). What the model needs is its own to say (`ds.ai.model.credential_problem`): a GitHub
  Copilot token for a `github-copilot:` model, the Gateway key for a `gateway/` one. `require_ai()` raises it, and every place that calls a model runs it first, so nothing is sent; the
  error shows where the user asked, as any failed call does. A new place that calls a model starts with it.
- **One rule hides the AI's controls**: the page's `data-ai` (from `State.ai_on`) and one CSS rule in
  `assets/app.css`: the ✨ buttons, the inline chat's boxes, the title bar's model and meters (Logfire
  isn't asked). `Alt+I` does nothing. The chat box stays: it runs the slash commands; a plain message gets
  one line saying it wasn't sent, and why.
- **The app starts without keys**: nothing read at import may need a key or a keyring service
  (`tests/services/ui/test_ai_switch.py` imports the app with neither).
- **Not covered**: `ds ai ...` in a terminal, and code a user writes in a cell that calls `ds.ai` itself.

## The model: one constant, and what follows from it

The user's rule (Nov 2026, branch `os-windows`): the model of every AI agent is one constant,
`DEFAULT_AI_MODEL` in `pkgs/ds/util/const.py`, and changing that line is all it takes.

- **One module knows the providers**: `pkgs/ds/ai/model.py`. `ai_model()` is what every `Agent(...)` gets
  (the chat agent, the inline chats, `/assign`, `from_url`, the script writer, the eval judge). A new agent
  is built with it, never with a model name of its own.
- **On `os-windows` the model is a GitHub Copilot one** (`github-copilot:gpt-5.6-luna`): the work laptop
  has a Copilot seat and nothing else. Its token is stored like the other keys (`ds settings sync`, which
  reads it from `gh auth token`; `Settings.github_copilot_token`) and read when a request is sent, so the
  app still starts with nothing stored.
- **Dollars are shown only where they are real** (`ds.ai.model.spend_tracked`: a `gateway/` model). A
  Copilot seat bills premium requests, which nothing here reads, so with a Copilot model these are not on
  the page: the Spend tab, the title bar's spend meters, the session's cost, and the cost in a usage line
  (it reads "1.2k in · 30 out · 1 request"). The context meter stays. No estimate takes their place.

- [omarchy.md](omarchy.md): navigation, keys and many other parts of the app follow Omarchy, the desktop
  it runs on.
- [inline_ai.md](inline_ai.md): `Alt+I`, the AI that changes what you are in. A widget with a tool is a
  function; the AI fills its inputs and the user runs them.
- [variables.md](variables.md): the Variables pane. Cleared means gone: one short undo, then the memory
  is really released. Also `@name` mentions of variables in the chats (experimental) and `/assign`, a variable whose code the AI writes.
